intro: Modal verbs have a second life: instead of obligation or ability, they can report the speaker's attitude to a claim. sollen in this 'subjective' use means 'is said to' — hearsay: Er soll reich sein (people say he's rich); Sie soll gewonnen haben (she's said to have won); Das Restaurant soll verkauft worden sein. And wollen means 'claims to': Er will nicht dort gewesen sein (he claims he wasn't there — and I doubt it). The form gives it away: soll / will in the present, with an infinitive for a present claim (reich sein) and a past infinitive — Partizip II + haben / sein — for a past one (gewonnen haben, gegangen sein). This is an introduction; later in the course you meet the whole subjective system (müssen = must be, dürfte = probably, könnte = might). sollen alone already covers what reading the news needs: recognising 'Der Minister soll zurücktreten' as a rumour, not an order.
tips[0].title: soll + infinitive = is said to
tips[0].text: Er soll reich sein. Das Hotel soll sehr gut sein. Die Firma soll Probleme haben. = Man sagt / Es heißt, dass … The speaker passes on what others say.
tips[0].trap: 'Er soll reich sein' is not 'he should be rich'. Objective sollen (should) usually has a person telling someone to do something; subjective sollen sits with sein / haben / a state and means rumour.
tips[0].check.why: soll + sein describing a state is hearsay: the speaker passes on what others say, it is not an obligation.
tips[1].title: Past claim: soll + Partizip II + haben / sein
tips[1].text: Sie soll gewonnen haben. Er soll nach Kanada gegangen sein. Er soll den Unfall verursacht haben. Passive: Das Restaurant soll geschlossen worden sein.
tips[1].check.why: A past rumour takes soll + Partizip II + helper, and zurücktreten forms its Perfekt with sein.
tips[2].title: will + infinitive = claims to (and I doubt it)
tips[2].text: Er will nicht dort gewesen sein (he claims he wasn't). Sie will den Minister kennen (she claims to know him). The subject makes the claim about themselves; the speaker is sceptical.
tips[2].check.why: When the subject makes the claim about himself, German uses will; soll would mean other people say so.
tips[3].title: sollen = others say; wollen = he says of himself
tips[3].text: Er soll reich sein (people say). Er will reich sein (he says so). Same structure, different source of the claim.
tips[3].check.why: wollen means the subject claims it about herself; with soll it would be other people talking.
tips[3].visual.rows[1].b: He claims he saw nothing (and I doubt it).
tips[3].visual.rows[2].a: Er soll das Geld gestohlen haben.
tips[3].visual.rows[2].b: He is said to have stolen the money.
remember[0]: soll + Infinitiv = is said to; soll + Partizip II + haben/sein = is said to have.
mistakes[0].why: Past infinitive needs the helper: gewesen sein.
mistakes[1].why: soll already means 'man sagt' — don't double it.
hook: Read the news like a native: spot when Er soll reich sein passes on a rumour and Er will … casts doubt on a claim.
tips[0].check.q: What does 'Das neue Café soll sehr gut sein' mean?
tips[0].check.options[0]: People say the new café is very good.
tips[0].check.options[1]: The new café should be very good.
tips[0].check.options[2]: The new café must be very good.
tips[0].check.answer: People say the new café is very good.
tips[3].check.q: 'Sie will das Buch allein geschrieben haben.' Who says she wrote it alone?
